title: Songs that will not leave
text: A song {{1}} itself in the mind, replays for hours and refuses eviction: researchers call these sticky tunes {{2}}, and surveys {{3}} that roughly ninety per cent of us are regularly visited. The recipes for a catchy earworm are surprisingly consistent: a {{4}} tempo, a simple melodic shape, and one small surprise the brain wants to resolve. Structure matters too — songs that stop {{5}} mid-phrase, as if interrupted, burrow in deepest, which is the same psychology that keeps us checking unfinished to-do lists; the mind {{6}} over incomplete business until it is closed. Escaping an earworm is famously difficult, and the remedies are comic. Chewing gum {{7}} the silent inner rehearsal of the lyrics and measurably weakens the loop; others solve anagrams or read a demanding novel to occupy the same mental channel. Mostly, though, sufferers simply wait, since time is the usual {{8}} and most earworms dissolve within hours. Curiously, the phenomenon says something flattering about us: a mind that rehearses music involuntarily is a mind built for patterns — the same machinery, pointed elsewhere, that learns languages and does arithmetic in the shower.

gaps.explanation: 'a song lodges itself in the mind' — sticks fast.
'researchers call them earworms' — the established term.
'surveys indicate that' — show; accuse, blame and protest are not neutral reporting verbs.
'a brisk tempo' — lively and quick; slow, plodding and sluggish would not catch in a catchy tune.
'songs that stop short mid-phrase' — halt abruptly; 'stop away', 'stop soon' and 'stop fast' are not idioms.
'the mind broods over unfinished business' — dwells on it.
'chewing gum disrupts the silent inner rehearsal' — breaks it up; enjoy, praise and memorise would feed the loop, not break it.
'time is the usual cure' — the remedy; symptom, disease and cause belong to the problem, not the fix.
